Privacy in SA: RICA v the Spies

By: Julian Sun | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How safe are you from being spied upon by the state?

Unique Selling Point:
The RICA act is the surveillance law that protects the average South African's right to privacy, but according to journalist unit AmaBhungane, the act does not do enough to protect South Africans from being spied upon by the State. They took their fight all the way to the Constitutional Court. Should it rule in their favour, it will have far reaching consequences for press freedom and privacy laws in South Africa.

Summary:
Investigative Unit Amabhungane launched a successful constitutional challenge against certain provisions of the RICA act in the high court in September 2019. This was after one of their members Sam Sole suspected that he was being spied upon by State Security. Sole is one of a number of journalists who believe their calls and metadata was monitored by the State, who manipulated provisions in the RICA acts in order to carry out this covert surveillance. The High Court's decision needs to be ratified by the Constitutional Court and the case was argued in Feb 2020. Should the court rule in favour of Amabhungane, it will have far reaching consequences for privacy in South Africa.

Press Release:


RICA: Privacy Under Attack?
The RICA legislation regulates the intercepting of communication – which a court has to order – to allow the state to listen in on the conversations of suspected criminals. Otherwise, two people talking on the phone have the right to privacy. So what happens when the government uses this legislation to spy on journalists? Carte Blanche retraces the events that have unfolded all the way to the Constitutional Court when investigative journalist Sam Sole found proof that he too was being spied on.
Producer: Julian Sun | Presenter: Masa Kekana


Script:


V/O: A free press is the cornerstone of a healthy, thriving democracy.

For a journalist, their sources provide a most important well of information

But what happens when they think that their phones are being bugged, their calls monitored and their movements tracked illicitly?

It all has something to do with a law called RICA.

MASA: We live in a country in which our freedom of expression and our right to privacy is enshrined in the constitution. But how would you feel if I told you that information about the phone calls I, you and everyone around me makes is potentially being monitored by the State as we speak?

V/O: The Regulation of Interception of Communications Act or RICA is a piece of South African legislation that governs the interception or monitoring of electronic communications.

Murray Hunter is the advocacy coordinator for the investigative journalism unit amaBhungane. He’s written extensively on the issue of surveillance in South Africa.

1. It’s been around since 2002 – written just after 9/11 when the world was worried about the potential impact of terrorism

2. RICA used when you’re suspected of being a criminal or you’re a threat to national security

V/O: The way RICA works is that if two people are having a phone conversation, they have the right to privacy and their communication cannot be monitored. But if criminal activity is suspected, the police or state security can apply to a designated judge for a surveillance warrant.

If that is granted, it allows them to listen in on all communications and the people who are targeted would never find out.






The problem is that there have been several instances where those targeted were not suspected criminals but rather investigative journalists.

V/O: Sam Sole is a managing partner at amaBhungane. When he was investigating former President Jacob Zuma, he began to suspect that his calls (and those of his colleague Stefans Brummer) were being monitored.

Comment from Sam – During the time that NPA were withdrawing charges against President Zuma there were rumours that I was being spied on

V/O: It’s one thing to suspect you’re being spied on another to have proof of it.

Amazingly in 2015, when the DA asked the High Court to release the Zuma spy tapes, he was able to obtain physical evidence that his calls were being recorded.

Then in 2015 when the DA was in court to get the spy tapes released, Michael Hulley (Zuma’s Lawyer) produced a transcript of a conversation that I had with NPA prosecutor Billy Downer – this was the first time I had physical proof that I was spied on

Sam’s comment on deciding to launch a court challenge

V/O: Sam Sole wasn’t the only journalist to be spied on. Media Freedom organization Right2Know published a report detailing several other cases as Thami Nkosi explains

Thami Nkosi lists other case studies

V/O: In the case of M&G journalist Athandiwe Saba, her cellphone records were obtained illegally.

Athandiwe comment

According to media professor Jane Duncan, this seemingly innocuous metadata can be used to build up a comprehensive picture of a person’s habits.

Jane Duncan on the power of metadata

V/O: In September 2019 amaBhungane launched their constitutional challenge to RICA in the North Gauteng High Court. Their attorney is Dario Milo

1. The need for post-notification after the surveillance has ended
2. Regulation on how the RICA judge is appointed
3. We want to know what happens to the information that’s been gathered.
4. Protection for journalists


V/O: Another crucial issue brought to the court’s attention concerns mass surveillance. It is alleged that the State Security Agency is sucking up large amounts of data from undersea fibre optic cables and internet networks.

The problem with mass surveillance


V/O: In a landmark judgement Judge Roland Sutherland ruled in amaBhungane’s favour striking down several provisions of RICA.

The judgement even attracted praise from Edward Snowden (who blew the whistle on the mass surveillance of its citizens, by the US Government)

Comments about the ruling

V/O: Judge Sutherland’s ruling still has to be ratified by the Constitutional Court and arguments were held last month

Comments from all about the concourt hearing –
The line of questioning of the concourt judges
The arguments put forward by the Ministries of Police & State Security

V/O: Carte Blanche approached the Department of Justice for comment but they declined, saying they don’t want to create an impression they’re pre-empting the decision of the court.



Comments about how long it will take for RICA to be reformed

TEASER PROMO: Journalist Sam Sole believed he was being monitored by the State. When he found proof, he began a journey that’s taken him all the way to the Constitutional Court in a fight for privacy and media freedom.

PROMO: The RICA act is the surveillance law that’s meant to protect the average South African’s right to privacy but could this legislation be used by the state to spy on citizens like you and me?


Promo 2: When does the state have the right to spy on its citizens? That‘s what investigative unit Amabhungane asked when it challenged RICA in the Constitutional Court, with profound implications for us all.

Promo 3: For a country that prides itself on freedom, South African journalists are fearful they’re being spied on. That’s because RICA, the law that’s meant to protect them is failing. How can this be fixed?
